questions.stem: Several children admitted on the specialist pediatric gastroenterology ward developed loose stool. One 11-month child still in diapers had diarrhea and a fever >38°C; another 3-year child had diarrhea and vomiting; and one 5-year old child had vomiting only. All three had been on the unit for 3 weeks, with an underlying diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease. Their symptoms began over a 48-hour period. Stool cultures for the 5-year-old were negative but were pending for the remaining two children. Blood results were unremarkable. Two staff members also reported vomiting over the preceding 24 hours.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Norovirus This fulfils Kaplan outbreak criteria for an outbreak as more than two patients related in time and space have developed similar symptoms. Norovirus is highly infectious and in this case has caused an outbreak. Although loose stool could be due to underlying inflammatory bowel disease in this population, vomiting is more indicative of norovirus, and even though the patients have been in hospital for 3 weeks, norovirus can often be introduced from the community, and the involvement of staff members here is highly suggestive. Accompanying fever is also commonly seen in norovirus infection, and there is no clear ingestion of a common food source to suggest Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus infection. Stool cultures should always be sent to exclude other enteric causes, and samples should also be tested for C. difficile as this can be commonly seen in patients with inflammatory bowel disease who receive multiple courses of antibiotics. Separate stool samples should be sent for norovirus as vomitus cannot be tested.

questions.question: Concern of a healthcare setting outbreak.

parts.text: Define outbreak.
What are 4 early steps in an outbreak.
What are 2 agents that kill norovirus?

parts_raw.text: Define outbreak.

questions.model_answer:
a) An outbreak is the occurrence of cases of a disease in a defined population, place and time period in excess of the expected/baseline number; in a healthcare setting a cluster of epidemiologically linked cases (often two or more) of a healthcare-associated infection above baseline, or even a single case of a never-event pathogen (e.g. hospital-acquired Legionella or group A streptococcus).
b) (1) Verify the diagnosis and confirm that a true excess over baseline exists. (2) Establish a working case definition (person, place, time, clinical/lab criteria) and actively case-find. (3) Line-list cases and construct an epidemic curve; describe by time, place and person. (4) Institute immediate control measures — appropriate additional precautions, cohorting, unit/admission restriction, enhanced cleaning, staff exclusion — and notify IPAC, administration and public health while assembling the outbreak management team.
c) (1) Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) 1000-5000 ppm available chlorine. (2) Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (or another virucidal agent with a demonstrated non-enveloped virus claim, e.g. hydrogen peroxide vapour); alcohol-based hand rub is NOT reliably effective — use soap and water.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC/Ontario PIDAC outbreak management and norovirus disinfection guidance.

questions.question: Norovirus infection in an institutional outbreak.

parts.text: List four initial steps to outbreak investigation.
What two cleaning agents should you use?
What are four things you need to do to ensure people are properly protected when wearing N95 respirators?

parts_raw.text: 4 initial steps to outbreak investigation (yes, 4)
What two cleaning agents should you use.
What are 4 things you need to do to ensure people are properly protected when wearing N95 respirators?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Confirm that an outbreak exists (cases above baseline) and verify the diagnosis with stool testing (norovirus RT-PCR) using the Kaplan criteria as a clinical guide. (2) Establish a case definition and construct a line list of cases by person, place and time; plot an epidemic curve. (3) Assemble the outbreak management team and notify public health/IPAC leadership. (4) Institute immediate control measures — contact precautions, cohorting of ill residents and staff, exclusion of ill staff until 48 hours after symptom resolution, closure of the unit to admissions/transfers, and enhanced environmental cleaning — while generating hypotheses about the source (point-source food/water versus person-to-person).
b) (1) Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) at 1000-5000 ppm available chlorine, and (2) an accelerated hydrogen peroxide product with a norovirus/non-enveloped virus claim; hand hygiene should use soap and water rather than alcohol-based rub, since alcohol is unreliable against norovirus.
c) (1) Medical clearance/fitness for respirator use. (2) Fit testing with the specific make, model and size before first use and repeated per policy. (3) Training in correct donning, doffing and safe removal, and in the limits of the respirator. (4) A user seal check (positive and negative pressure) performed every time the respirator is put on, with no facial hair or anything that breaks the seal, and correct selection of a certified N95 that has been fit tested for that individual.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC Routine Practices and Additional Precautions (2017) and PIDAC norovirus outbreak guidance; CSA Z94.4 respirator program (medical clearance, fit testing, training, seal check).

questions.model_answer: a) Caliciviridae. b) RNA (positive-sense, nonenveloped). c) Single-stranded. d) (1) Contact precautions for symptomatic residents (add droplet precautions when vomiting), placing the resident in a private room. (2) Hand hygiene with soap and water (alcohol-based rub is less reliable against norovirus) plus environmental decontamination with a chlorine/bleach-based agent.

questions.model_answer:
a) Vibrio vulnificus.
b) (1) Primary septicemia (abrupt chills/fever, hypotension, metastatic hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions) following raw-oyster ingestion (2) Rapidly progressive necrotizing wound infection/cellulitis after seawater exposure (3) Acute self-limited diarrheal illness.
c) (1) Cirrhosis/underlying liver disease (2) Iron-overload states (hemochromatosis, hemolytic anemia, chronic renal failure) (3) Malignancy, HIV infection, or immunosuppressive medications.
d) (1) Norovirus (2) Hepatitis A virus.

questions.model_answer: a) 24-48 hours (range approximately 12-72 hours). b) Acute-onset nausea, vomiting, watery non-bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps, often with low-grade fever, myalgia and malaise; self-limited, lasting 12-72 hours (typically 24-72 hours) with rapid recovery. c) RT-PCR of stool (most sensitive; also detects virus in vomitus/environmental samples). d) Very low infectious dose (<100 viral particles) combined with high environmental stability, resistance to alcohol-based hand sanitizers and many disinfectants, prolonged/asymptomatic shedding, and aerosolization of virus from vomitus.

questions.model_answer: a) 24-48 hours (range approximately 18-72 hours). b) Nausea, non-bloody vomiting, watery non-bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps, with prominent myalgia, malaise and headache; fever in about half of cases. Self-limited, typically lasting 48-72 hours with rapid recovery. c) High infectivity from a very low infectious dose (<100 particles), prolonged asymptomatic viral shedding (weeks after recovery), environmental stability, and resistance to many disinfectants including alcohol and moderate heat/chlorine; lack of durable immunity also permits reinfection.
questions.beyond_mandell: Provided context file was the Rhinovirus chapter, not Norovirus; answered from Mandell norovirus content and CDC guidance.

cohort_answer.text:
Incubation period: Approximately 24-48 hours, although ranges from 18 to 72 hours have been observed.
Symptoms and duration: Nausea, vomiting (non-bloody, non-bilious), watery diarrhea (non-bloody) with abdominal pain; generalized myalgias, malaise, headache prominent; fever in approximately half of cases. Symptoms typically last 48-72 hours with rapid recovery.
Why challenging to prevent spread: High infectivity with low infectious dose (<100 viral particles required); asymptomatic shedding (mean duration of viral shedding 4 weeks after onset of illness); environmental stability (resists freezing, heating to 60°C, disinfection with chlorine/alcohol).

questions.model_answer: a) 24-48 hours (range 18-72 hours). b) Prominent nausea and vomiting with watery non-bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps and low-grade fever; typically lasts 12-60 hours (viral shedding maximal in the first 24-48 hours after onset). c) RT-PCR for norovirus in stool. d) Environmental stability with resistance to inactivation by chlorine, alcohol and heating/cooling; a very small infectious inoculum (<100 particles); presymptomatic and asymptomatic food handlers; and airborne/droplet transmission from aerosolized vomit.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Generally 24-48 hours, but range is 18-72 hours.

B: Often nausea/vomiting prominent, along with diarrhea; abdominal cramps and low grade fever may be present. Duration usually 12-60 hours. Viral shedding maximal for first 24-48 hours after illness.

C: rt-PCR for virus in stool.

D: Resistance to inactivation with chlorine, alcohol and heat/cooling. Environmental stability. Small inoculum required for transmission (<100 particles). Role of pre-symptomatic food handlers in spreading disease. Potential role of airborne droplet transmission via vomit.

questions.model_answer: a) A single-stranded, positive-sense, nonenveloped RNA virus of the family Caliciviridae (genus Norovirus). b) Fecal-oral, with fomites and contaminated food/water (often via infected food handlers) contributing to a high secondary attack rate; aerosolization of vomitus also transmits. c) (1) Exclude ill food handlers/staff from work until 48-72 hours after symptom resolution and identify/eliminate the common source. (2) Hand washing with soap and water (not reliably killed by alcohol-based rubs) plus environmental decontamination with concentrated bleach; contact precautions in hospital. d) RT-PCR of stool is most sensitive; ELISA/antigen detection has reduced sensitivity; electron microscopy is insensitive and no longer used.
questions.beyond_mandell: Provided context file was the Rhinovirus chapter, not Norovirus; answered from Mandell norovirus content.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Family Caliciviridae, genera Norovirus and Sapovirus. ss, positive sense, non-enveloped RNA virus; each has multiple genogroups and genotypes

B: Fecal-oral, with fomites and contaminated food/water by food handlers contributing to infectivity and high secondary attack rate. Implicated foods include sandwiches and salads, particularly salad greens.

C: Excluding ill employees from work until 48-72 hours after symptom resolution; identify and eliminate common sources; use hand washing and barrier methods (not killed by alcohol based hand disinfection); decontaminate fomites with concentrated bleach or other approved solution; use contact precautions in hospital.

D: rt-PCR for virus in stool most sensitive. ELISA has reduced sensitivity. Electron microscopy no longer used.
